notes.front: What is the basic description of a hazardous material on a shipping paper?
notes.back: Its identification number, proper shipping name, hazard class or division, and packing group, shown in that sequence.
notes.explanation: Section 172.202(b) requires these four entries to be shown in sequence with no additional information placed between them.
notes.example: Like the fixed order of a postal address (street, town, postcode), but for a hazardous material: number, name, class, then packing group.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.202(a)–(b), PDF p. 235
notes.evidence: the basic description specified in paragraphs (a)(1), (2), (3), and (4) of this section must be shown in sequence with no additional information interspersed.

notes.front: What is the shipper's certification?
notes.back: A statement the offeror prints on the shipping paper certifying that the hazardous material is offered in accordance with the regulations.
notes.explanation: Section 172.204(a) requires it to be printed, manually or mechanically, on the shipping paper that carries the required shipping description.
notes.example: Like signing a customs declaration that a parcel holds what it says, but made by the shipper about how a hazardous material was classed, described, packaged, marked and labelled.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.204(a), PDF p. 240
notes.evidence: each person who offers a hazardous material for transportation shall certify that the material is offered for transportation in accordance with this subchapter by printing (manually or mechanically) on the shipping paper containing the required shipping description

notes.front: Under § 172.200(a), who must describe a hazardous material on a shipping paper?
notes.back: Each person who offers the hazardous material for transportation, except as the subpart provides otherwise.
notes.explanation: The duty sits with the offeror; paragraph (b) then takes some materials out of the shipping paper subpart altogether.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.200(a)–(b), PDF p. 233
notes.evidence: a hazardous material for transportation shall describe the hazardous material on the shipping paper in the manner required by this subpart. (b) This subpart does not apply to any material

notes.front: May a highway carrier accept a hazardous material that arrives without a shipping paper?
notes.back: No, unless the material is excepted from the shipping paper requirements.
notes.explanation: Section 177.817(a) bars both accepting and transporting it by highway until the person has received a shipping paper prepared under part 172.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 177 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 177.817(a), PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: A person may not accept a hazardous material for transportation or transport a hazardous material by highway unless that person has received a shipping paper prepared in accordance with part 172 of this subchapter or the material is excepted from shipping paper requirements under this subchapter.

notes.front: A driver arrives to collect six drums of a regulated flammable liquid, but the shipper has not printed the paperwork yet and offers to send it tomorrow. What does § 177.817 require?
notes.back: B: The driver may not accept the drums until a shipping paper has been received.
notes.choices:
A) The driver may take the drums if they are already marked and labelled
B) The driver may not accept the drums until a shipping paper has been received
C) The driver may take the drums if the description is emailed within a day
D) The driver may take the drums, since only the offeror has shipping paper duties
notes.choicesExplained: A: Marks and labels do not replace the shipping paper the carrier must receive. C: Sending the description later does not meet a rule that applies at acceptance. D: Section 177.817(a) binds the person accepting and transporting the material too.
notes.explanation: The carrier needs the shipping paper at acceptance, not afterwards, unless the material is excepted.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 177 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 177.817(a), PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: A person may not accept a hazardous material for transportation or transport a hazardous material by highway unless that person has received a shipping paper

notes.front: A material has the letter A in column 1 of the Hazardous Materials Table. When does the shipping paper subpart apply to it?
notes.back: Only when it is offered or intended for transportation by air, unless it is a hazardous substance, hazardous waste or marine pollutant.
notes.explanation: Paragraph (b)(1) lifts the subpart from these materials for other modes, but the lift never covers a hazardous substance, hazardous waste or marine pollutant.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.200(b)(1), PDF p. 233
notes.evidence: This subpart does not apply to any material, other than a hazardous substance, hazardous waste or marine pollutant, that is— (1) Identified by the letter ‘‘A’’ in column 1 of the § 172.101 table, except when the material is offered or intended for transportation by air; or

notes.front: A material has the letter W in column 1 of the Hazardous Materials Table. When does the shipping paper subpart apply to it?
notes.back: Only when it is offered or intended for transportation by water, unless it is a hazardous substance, hazardous waste or marine pollutant.
notes.explanation: Paragraph (b)(2) mirrors the rule for letter A materials, with water in place of air.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.200(b)(2), PDF p. 233
notes.evidence: (2) Identified by the letter ‘‘W’’ in column 1 of the § 172.101 table, except when the material is offered or intended for transportation by water; or

notes.front: When does a limited quantity package need a shipping paper?
notes.back: When the material is offered for transportation by aircraft or vessel.
notes.explanation: Paragraph (b)(3) takes limited quantity packages out of the subpart for other modes, such as highway and rail.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.200(b)(3), PDF p. 233
notes.evidence: (3) A limited quantity package unless the material is offered for transportation by aircraft or vessel.

notes.front: Which infectious substances does § 172.200(b) take out of the shipping paper subpart?
notes.back: Category B infectious substances prepared in accordance with § 173.199.
notes.explanation: The exception depends on the packaging rules of § 173.199 being met, not on the class alone.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.200(b)(4), PDF p. 233
notes.evidence: (4) Category B infectious substances prepared in accordance with § 173.199.

notes.front: A distributor sends two consignments of a flammable liquid packed as limited quantities: one by truck, one by container ship. Neither is a hazardous substance, waste or marine pollutant. Which needs a shipping paper?
notes.back: D: Only the container ship consignment.
notes.choices:
A) Both consignments
B) Neither consignment
C) Only the truck consignment
D) Only the container ship consignment
notes.choicesExplained: A: The truck consignment is excepted. B: The vessel consignment is not excepted. C: This reverses the rule: highway is the excepted mode here.
notes.explanation: The limited quantity exception from shipping papers stops where transport by aircraft or vessel begins.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.200(b)(3), PDF p. 233
notes.evidence: (3) A limited quantity package unless the material is offered for transportation by aircraft or vessel.

notes.front: A shipping paper lists hazardous and non-hazardous materials. Which placement of the hazardous entries meets § 172.201(a)(1) by position alone?
notes.back: Entering them first, before the materials not subject to the regulations.
notes.explanation: The rule covers the § 172.202 description entries and any additional entries required by § 172.203.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.201(a)(1)(i), PDF p. 233
notes.evidence: When a hazardous material and a material not subject to the requirements of this subchapter are described on the same shipping paper, the hazardous material description entries required by § 172.202 and those additional entries that may be required by § 172.203: (i) Must be entered first, or

notes.front: On a mixed shipping paper, how can colour set the hazardous material entries apart?
notes.back: Print them in a colour that clearly contrasts with the other descriptions; on a reproduction they may be highlighted instead.
notes.explanation: The colour method covers only the four entries of the basic description, not the other entries.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.201(a)(1)(ii), PDF p. 233
notes.evidence: (ii) Must be entered in a color that clearly contrasts with any description on the shipping paper of a material not subject to the requirements of this subchapter, except that a description on a reproduction of a shipping paper may be highlighted, rather than printed, in a contrasting color (the provisions of this paragraph apply only to the basic description

notes.front: On a mixed shipping paper, what column entry can identify a hazardous material?
notes.back: An X before its basic description in a column captioned `HM`; the X may be replaced by `RQ` where appropriate.
notes.explanation: This is the third accepted method, used instead of listing the hazardous entries first or in a contrasting colour.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.201(a)(1)(iii), PDF p. 233
notes.evidence: (iii) Must be identified by the entry of an ‘‘X’’ placed before the basic shipping description required by § 172.202 in a column captioned ‘‘HM.’’ (The ‘‘X’’ may be replaced by ‘‘RQ,’’ if appropriate.)

notes.front: A bill of lading lists office paper, then a corrosive liquid, then printer toner, all in black ink with no special columns. What is wrong with it?
notes.back: B: The corrosive entry is not first, not in a contrasting colour and not marked in a hazardous materials column.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, as long as the corrosive description is complete
B) The corrosive entry is not first, not in a contrasting colour and not marked in a hazardous materials column
C) The non-hazardous items must go on a separate shipping paper
D) The corrosive liquid must be listed last
notes.choicesExplained: A: A complete description is not enough on a mixed paper; it must also stand out. C: Mixing is allowed; the rule sets how the hazardous entries are distinguished. D: Listing it first is a method; listing it last is not.
notes.explanation: Section 172.201(a)(1) requires one of those three methods whenever hazardous and other materials share a shipping paper.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.201(a)(1), PDF p. 233
notes.evidence: When a hazardous material and a material not subject to the requirements of this subchapter are described on the same shipping paper, the hazardous material description entries required by § 172.202 and those additional entries that may be required by § 172.203: (i) Must be entered first, or

notes.front: In what language and form must the shipping description on a shipping paper be?
notes.back: Legible and printed, manually or mechanically, in English, on the paper and every copy used for transportation.
notes.explanation: The rule covers all copies used for transportation purposes, not only the original.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.201(a)(2), PDF p. 233
notes.evidence: (2) The required shipping description on a shipping paper and all copies of the shipping paper used for transportation purposes must be legible and printed (manually or mechanically) in English.

notes.front: Unless specifically authorised or required by the regulations, the required shipping description may not contain any {{c1::code or abbreviation}}.
notes.explanation: The exception is narrow: a short form is acceptable only where the subchapter itself authorises or requires it.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.201(a)(3), PDF p. 233
notes.evidence: (3) Unless it is specifically authorized or required in this subchapter, the required shipping description may not contain any code or abbreviation.

notes.front: A shipper prints the shipping description in clear Spanish only, because the driver and the consignee both read Spanish. Does the shipping paper comply?
notes.back: C: No; the required shipping description must be printed in English.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if an English copy is kept at the principal place of business
B) Yes, because the people handling it can read it
C) No; the required shipping description must be printed in English
D) No; the description must be handwritten
notes.choicesExplained: B: Being legible to the readers is not enough; the language is set. A: The copies used for transportation must also be in English. D: Printing may be manual or mechanical.
notes.explanation: The English requirement does not depend on who reads the paper.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.201(a)(2), PDF p. 233
notes.evidence: (2) The required shipping description on a shipping paper and all copies of the shipping paper used for transportation purposes must be legible and printed (manually or mechanically) in English.

notes.front: How must a shipping paper of more than one page be numbered?
notes.back: Each page numbered consecutively, with the first page showing the total, for example "Page 1 of 4 pages".
notes.explanation: Every page carries its number, and the first page also carries the total.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.201(c), PDF p. 234
notes.evidence: A shipping paper may consist of more than one page, if each page is consecutively numbered and the first page bears a notation specifying the total number of pages included in the shipping paper.

notes.front: How long must the person who provides a shipping paper keep a copy, for a hazardous material that is not hazardous waste?
notes.back: Two years after the material is accepted by the initial carrier.
notes.explanation: The period runs from acceptance by the initial carrier; hazardous waste copies are kept three years.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.201(e), PDF p. 234
notes.evidence: For a hazardous waste, the shipping paper copy must be retained for three years after the material is accepted by the initial carrier. For all other hazardous materials, the shipping paper must be retained for two years after the material is accepted by the initial carrier.

notes.front: How long must a shipping paper copy for a hazardous waste be kept?
notes.back: Three years after the waste is accepted by the initial carrier.
notes.explanation: That is one year longer than the two years for other hazardous materials.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.201(e), PDF p. 234
notes.evidence: For a hazardous waste, the shipping paper copy must be retained for three years after the material is accepted by the initial carrier. For all other hazardous materials, the shipping paper must be retained for two years after the material is accepted by the initial carrier.

notes.front: Under § 177.817(f), how long must a highway carrier keep its copy of a shipping paper for a material other than hazardous waste, compared with the offeror?
notes.back: One year after the carrier accepts the material; the offeror keeps its copy two years. Hazardous waste is three years for both.
notes.explanation: The carrier’s one-year period runs from its acceptance of the material; hazardous waste stays at three years.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 177 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 177.817(f), PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: For a hazardous waste, the shipping paper copy must be retained for three years after the material is accepted by the initial carrier. For all other hazardous materials, the shipping paper copy must be retained for one year after the material is accepted by the carrier.

notes.front: A chemical maker shipped a drum of corrosive liquid, not a waste, which the first carrier accepted 20 months ago. An inspector now asks the maker for the shipping paper. What applies?
notes.back: C: The maker must still keep the copy.
notes.choices:
A) The maker could have discarded it after one year
B) The maker need keep it only if the drum was involved in an incident
C) The maker must still keep the copy
D) Only the carrier must keep a copy
notes.choicesExplained: A: One year is the highway carrier’s period under § 177.817(f), not the offeror’s. B: Retention does not depend on an incident. D: The person who provides the shipping paper must keep a copy too.
notes.explanation: Twenty months is inside the offeror’s two-year period, which runs from acceptance by the initial carrier.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.201(e), PDF p. 234
notes.evidence: For all other hazardous materials, the shipping paper must be retained for two years after the material is accepted by the initial carrier.

notes.front: A new clerk writes a description with the proper shipping name first, then the identification number, the hazard class and the packing group. How should it be reordered?
notes.back: A: Identification number, proper shipping name, hazard class, packing group.
notes.choices:
A) Identification number, proper shipping name, hazard class, packing group
B) Hazard class, identification number, proper shipping name, packing group
C) Proper shipping name, hazard class, packing group, identification number
D) Identification number, hazard class, proper shipping name, packing group
notes.choicesExplained: C: The identification number comes first, not last. B: The hazard class is third. D: The proper shipping name comes before the hazard class.
notes.explanation: The four entries of the basic description follow the order of § 172.202(a)(1) to (a)(4).
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.202(a), PDF p. 234
notes.evidence: (1) The identification number prescribed for the material as shown in Column (4) of the § 172.101 table; (2) The proper shipping name prescribed for the material in Column (2) of the § 172.101 table; (3) The hazard class or division number prescribed for the material

notes.front: Where does a subsidiary hazard class go in the shipping description?
notes.back: In parentheses immediately after the primary hazard class or division number.
notes.explanation: It may be left out when no subsidiary hazard label is required, and the parentheses rule does not apply to combustible liquids.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.202(a)(3), PDF p. 234
notes.evidence: The subsidiary hazard class or division number is not required to be entered when a corresponding subsidiary hazard label is not required. Except for combustible liquids, the subsidiary hazard class(es) or subsidiary division number(s) must be entered in parentheses immediately following the primary hazard class or division number.

notes.front: A liquid has primary hazard Division 6.1 and subsidiary hazards of Class 8 and Class 3, each needing a label. How is the class written in its description?
notes.choicesExplained: A: The subsidiary numbers must be in parentheses. B: The parentheses go round the subsidiary numbers, not the primary one. C: The primary division, 6.1, must come first.
notes.explanation: The primary division comes first, with the subsidiary numbers in parentheses straight after it.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.202(a)(3), PDF p. 234
notes.evidence: the subsidiary hazard class(es) or subsidiary division number(s) must be entered in parentheses immediately following the primary hazard class or division number.

notes.front: How is the packing group shown in the basic description?
notes.back: In Roman numerals, as designated in column 5 of the Hazardous Materials Table.
notes.explanation: Class 1, self-reactive and Division 5.2 materials, and entries with no packing group, are excepted from this entry.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.202(a)(4), PDF p. 234
notes.evidence: (4) The packing group in Roman numerals, as designated for the hazardous material in Column (5) of the § 172.101 table. Class 1 (explosives) materials; self-reactive substances; Division 5.2 materials; and entries that are not assigned a packing group (e.g., Class 7) are excepted from this requirement.

notes.front: Four descriptions are being checked. Which of these shipments has no packing group entry in its basic description?
notes.back: D: Division 5.2 organic peroxide
notes.choices:
A) Corrosive liquid, Class 8, packing group I
B) Flammable liquid, Class 3, packing group II
C) Toxic solid, Division 6.1, packing group III
D) Division 5.2 organic peroxide
notes.choicesExplained: A: Class 8 materials are assigned packing groups, so PG I must be shown. B: Class 3 materials are assigned packing groups, so PG II must be shown. C: Division 6.1 materials are assigned packing groups, so PG III must be shown.
notes.explanation: Division 5.2 materials are named among those excepted from the packing group entry.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.202(a)(4), PDF p. 234
notes.evidence: Class 1 (explosives) materials; self-reactive substances; Division 5.2 materials; and entries that are not assigned a packing group (e.g., Class 7) are excepted from this requirement.

notes.front: Except for air transport, what quantity must the shipping description show?
notes.back: The total quantity covered by the description, by mass or volume (activity for Class 7), with its unit of measurement.
notes.explanation: The unit is part of the requirement: the section gives "200 kg" and "50 L" as examples.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.202(a)(5), PDF p. 235
notes.evidence: (5) Except for transportation by aircraft, the total quantity of hazardous materials covered by the description must be indicated (by mass or volume, or by activity for Class 7 materials) and must include an indication of the applicable unit of measurement, for example, ‘‘200 kg’’ (440 pounds) or ‘‘50 L’’ (13 gallons).

notes.front: For Class 1 materials, the quantity on the shipping paper must be the {{c1::net explosive mass}}.
notes.explanation: For an explosive article, the net explosive mass may be expressed as the net mass of the article or of the explosive in it.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.202(a)(5)(i), PDF p. 235
notes.evidence: (i) For Class 1 materials, the quantity must be the net explosive mass. For an explosive that is an article, such as Cartridges, small arms, the net explosive mass may be expressed in terms of the net mass of either the article or the explosive materials contained in the article.

notes.front: What quantity entry is enough for bulk packages and for cylinders?
notes.back: Some indication of the total quantity, such as "1 cargo tank" or "10 cylinders".
notes.explanation: These, with packages containing only residue, are excepted from the full quantity entry.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.202(a)(5)(iii), PDF p. 235
notes.evidence: (A) Bulk packages, provided some indication of the total quantity is shown, for example, ‘‘1 cargo tank’’ or ‘‘2 IBCs.’’ (B) Cylinders, provided some indication of the total quantity is shown, for example, ‘‘10 cylinders.’’ (C) Packages containing only residue.

notes.front: A shipper sends 40 pails of a Class 8 liquid by truck, each holding 20 litres. Which total quantity entry meets § 172.202(a)(5)?
notes.choices:
A) 40
B) Corrosive
C) Several pails
D) 800 L
notes.choicesExplained: A: A bare number has no unit of measurement. B: That is a hazard, not a quantity. C: That gives neither a total nor a unit.
notes.explanation: The entry is the total quantity with its unit of measurement.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.202(a)(5), PDF p. 235
notes.evidence: the total quantity of hazardous materials covered by the description must be indicated (by mass or volume, or by activity for Class 7 materials) and must include an indication of the applicable unit of measurement

notes.front: How must the number and type of packages be shown on a shipping paper?
notes.back: By describing them, for example "12 drums"; the packaging specification code may be added.
notes.explanation: The packaging specification code, such as 1H1, is optional; the description of the package is not.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.202(a)(7), PDF p. 235
notes.evidence: (7) The number and type of packages must be indicated. The type of packages must be indicated by description of the package (for example, ‘‘12 drums’’). Indication of the packaging specification number (‘‘1H1’’) may be included in the description of the package

notes.front: A clerk is filling in the package column for five steel drums. Which entry meets § 172.202(a)(7)?
notes.back: C: 5 drums
notes.choices:
A) 5
B) Steel
C) 5 drums
D) Drums
notes.choicesExplained: A: The type of package is missing. B: The number and the package type are missing. D: The number is missing.
notes.explanation: The entry needs both the count and a description of the package type.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.202(a)(7), PDF p. 235
notes.evidence: The number and type of packages must be indicated. The type of packages must be indicated by description of the package (for example, ‘‘12 drums’’).

notes.front: When a shipping paper is required for a limited quantity, what words must follow the basic description?
notes.back: "Limited Quantity" or "Ltd Qty".
notes.explanation: The words follow the basic description instead of being placed inside it.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.203(b), PDF p. 236
notes.evidence: When a shipping paper is required by this subchapter, the description for a material offered for transportation as ‘‘limited quantity,’’ as authorized by this subchapter, must include the words ‘‘Limited Quantity’’ or ‘‘Ltd Qty’’ following the basic description.

notes.front: A flammable liquid packed as a limited quantity is booked on an aircraft, so a shipping paper is prepared. Where does the limited quantity notation go?
notes.back: C: Immediately following the basic description.
notes.choices:
A) Only on the package, never on the paper
B) Before the identification number
C) Immediately following the basic description
D) Between the proper shipping name and the hazard class
notes.choicesExplained: B: The words follow the basic description; they do not open it. A: When a shipping paper is required, the description must include the words. D: Nothing may be interspersed within the basic description.
notes.explanation: Because a shipping paper is required, the description must carry "Limited Quantity" or "Ltd Qty" after the basic description.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.203(b), PDF p. 236
notes.evidence: must include the words ‘‘Limited Quantity’’ or ‘‘Ltd Qty’’ following the basic description.

notes.front: Where must the letters `RQ` go on a shipping paper describing a hazardous substance?
notes.back: Either before or after the basic description.
notes.explanation: The letters are required for each hazardous substance described on the paper.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.203(c)(2), PDF p. 236
notes.evidence: (2) The letters ‘‘RQ’’ must be entered on the shipping paper either before or after the basic description required by § 172.202 for each hazardous substance

notes.front: A clerk describing a hazardous substance places `RQ` between the proper shipping name and the hazard class. Is that right?
notes.back: A: No; it must be entered before or after the basic description.
notes.choices:
A) No; it must be entered before or after the basic description
B) Yes; it belongs next to the proper shipping name
C) No; it belongs only on the package, not the paper
D) Yes, provided the notation is in a contrasting colour
notes.choicesExplained: B: The rule gives only two places, before or after. C: Section 172.203(c)(2) puts it on the shipping paper. D: Colour does not change where the letters go.
notes.explanation: The rule offers only two positions: before or after the basic description.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.203(c)(2), PDF p. 236
notes.evidence: (2) The letters ‘‘RQ’’ must be entered on the shipping paper either before or after the basic description required by § 172.202 for each hazardous substance

notes.front: If the proper shipping name of a hazardous substance does not name the substance, what must be added to the description?
notes.back: The substance’s name in parentheses with the basic description; for two or more, at least the two with the lowest reportable quantities.
notes.explanation: Nothing is added when the proper shipping name already identifies the hazardous substance by name.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.203(c)(1), PDF p. 236
notes.evidence: does not identify the hazardous substance by name, the name of the hazardous substance must be entered in parentheses in association with the basic description. If the material contains two or more hazardous substances, at least two hazardous substances, including the two with the lowest reportable quantities (RQs), must be identified.

notes.front: What words may describe a packaging that holds only the residue of a hazardous material?
notes.back: "RESIDUE: Last Contained * * *", immediately before or after the basic description.
notes.explanation: For an ordinary packaging the phrase is optional; for a tank car it is required.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.203(e), PDF p. 237
notes.evidence: (1) The description on the shipping paper for a packaging containing the residue of a hazardous material may include the words ‘‘RESIDUE: Last Contained * * *’’ immediately before or after the basic shipping description on the shipping paper. (2) The description on the shipping paper for a tank car containing the residue of a hazardous material must include

notes.front: An emptied, uncleaned tote that last held a flammable liquid (not a tank car) goes back to the supplier with a shipping paper. Which statement about "RESIDUE: Last Contained" is right?
notes.back: A: It may be used, immediately before or after the basic description.
notes.choices:
A) It may be used, immediately before or after the basic description
B) It must replace the proper shipping name
C) It must be used for every packaging holding residue
D) It may not appear on a shipping paper
notes.choicesExplained: C: Must applies only to tank cars. B: The phrase is added before or after the description; it does not replace the name. D: Section 172.203(e) expressly allows it.
notes.explanation: Only a tank car description must include the phrase; for other packagings it is optional.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.203(e)(1), PDF p. 237
notes.evidence: (1) The description on the shipping paper for a packaging containing the residue of a hazardous material may include the words ‘‘RESIDUE: Last Contained * * *’’ immediately before or after the basic shipping description on the shipping paper.

notes.front: When must a technical name be entered in parentheses with the basic description?
notes.back: When the proper shipping name is one marked with the letter G in column 1 of the Hazardous Materials Table, unless excepted.
notes.explanation: Section 172.203(k) applies this to n.o.s. and other generic descriptions.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.203(k), PDF p. 238
notes.evidence: (k) Technical names for ‘‘n.o.s.’’ and other generic descriptions. Unless otherwise excepted, if a material is described on a shipping paper by one of the proper shipping names identified by the letter ‘‘G’’ in column (1) of the § 172.101 Table, the technical name of the hazardous material must be entered in parentheses in association with the basic description.

notes.front: A blend of two flammable, hazardous solvents is shipped under a "Flammable liquids, n.o.s." entry marked G in column 1. What goes in parentheses with the description?
notes.back: B: The technical names of at least the two components contributing most to its hazards.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing; an n.o.s. entry needs no further detail
B) The technical names of at least the two components contributing most to its hazards
C) The shipper’s product code
D) The trade name of the blend
notes.choicesExplained: A: Entries marked G need a technical name. D: A trade name is not a technical name. C: Codes may not be used in the description unless authorised.
notes.explanation: For a mixture of two or more hazardous materials, one technical name is not enough.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.203(k)(1), PDF p. 239
notes.evidence: (1) If a hazardous material is a mixture or solution of two or more hazardous materials, the technical names of at least two components most predominately contributing to the hazards of the mixture or solution must be entered on the shipping paper

notes.front: What must follow the shipping description of a material poisonous by inhalation?
notes.back: "Poison-Inhalation Hazard" or "Toxic-Inhalation Hazard", plus the zone: Zone A to D for gases, Zone A or B for liquids.
notes.explanation: The zones differ by physical state: gases can fall in any of four zones, liquids in only two.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.203(m), PDF p. 240
notes.evidence: the words ‘‘PoisonInhalation Hazard’’ or ‘‘Toxic-Inhalation Hazard’’ and the words ‘‘Zone A’’, ‘‘Zone B’’, ‘‘Zone C’’, or ‘‘Zone D’’ for gases or ‘‘Zone A’’ or ‘‘Zone B’’ for liquids, as appropriate, shall be entered on the shipping paper immediately following the shipping description.

notes.front: A cylinder of a gas poisonous by inhalation, in Hazard Zone C, is being described on a shipping paper. What must be added?
notes.back: B: The inhalation hazard words and the zone, immediately following the shipping description.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing; the division number shows the hazard
B) The inhalation hazard words and the zone, immediately following the shipping description
C) The zone only, before the identification number
D) The inhalation hazard words only, on the package
notes.choicesExplained: A: The division alone does not meet § 172.203(m). C: Both the words and the zone are needed, after the description. D: This rule is about the shipping paper, and the zone is required too.
notes.explanation: Both the words and the zone are entered right after the shipping description.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.203(m), PDF p. 240
notes.evidence: for gases or ‘‘Zone A’’ or ‘‘Zone B’’ for liquids, as appropriate, shall be entered on the shipping paper immediately following the shipping description.

notes.front: The § 172.204(a)(1) certification reads: "This is to certify that the above-named materials are properly classified, described, packaged, marked and labeled, and are {{c1::in proper condition for transportation}} according to the applicable regulations of the Department of Transportation."
notes.explanation: The words "herein-named" may be used in place of "above-named"; the alternative declaration in (a)(2) is also accepted.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.204(a)(1), PDF p. 240
notes.evidence: ‘‘This is to certify that the abovenamed materials are properly classified, described, packaged, marked and labeled, and are in proper condition for transportation according to the applicable regulations of the Department of Transportation.’’ NOTE: In line one of the certification the words ‘‘herein-named’’ may be substituted for the words ‘‘above-named’’.

notes.front: Who may sign the shipper's certification, and how?
notes.back: A principal, officer, partner or employee of the shipper or its agent, legibly, by hand, typewriter or other mechanical means.
notes.explanation: The signature need not be handwritten, but it must be legible.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.204(d), PDF p. 242
notes.evidence: (1) Must be legibly signed by a principal, officer, partner, or employee of the shipper or his agent; and (2) May be legibly signed manually, by typewriter, or by other mechanical means.

notes.front: A logistics firm acting as the shipper's agent prepares a shipping paper, and one of its employees' names is printed mechanically in the certification's signature space. Is that acceptable?
notes.back: C: Yes; an employee of the shipper’s agent may sign, and mechanical signing is allowed.
notes.choices:
A) No; it must be signed by hand in ink
B) No; only an officer of the shipper may sign
C) Yes; an employee of the shipper’s agent may sign, and mechanical signing is allowed
D) Yes, but only if the carrier countersigns it
notes.choicesExplained: A: Signing by typewriter or other mechanical means is allowed. B: Employees and agents may sign too. D: No carrier countersignature is required.
notes.explanation: Both the signer and the method fall within § 172.204(d).
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.204(d), PDF p. 242
notes.evidence: (1) Must be legibly signed by a principal, officer, partner, or employee of the shipper or his agent; and (2) May be legibly signed manually, by typewriter, or by other mechanical means.

notes.front: What are two highway situations in which no shipper’s certification is required?
notes.back: A cargo tank supplied by the carrier; carriage by the shipper as a private carrier, unless reshipped. Neither applies to hazardous waste.
notes.explanation: Private carriage keeps the exception only while the material is not reshipped or transferred to another carrier.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.204(b), PDF p. 241
notes.evidence: (1) Except for a hazardous waste, no certification is required for a hazardous material offered for transportation by motor vehicle and transported: (i) In a cargo tank supplied by the carrier, or (ii) By the shipper as a private carrier except for a hazardous material that is to be reshipped or transferred from one carrier to another.

notes.front: May an initial highway carrier accept a shipment whose shipping paper has no shipper's certification?
notes.back: No, unless it is excepted, as private carriage or a carrier-supplied bulk cargo tank are, other than for hazardous waste.
notes.explanation: The check falls on the initial carrier, at the point of acceptance.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 177 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 177.817(b), PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: An initial carrier may not accept a hazardous material offered for transportation unless the shipping paper describing the material includes a shipper’s certification which meets the requirements in § 172.204 of this subchapter. Except for a hazardous waste, the certification is not required for shipments to be transported entirely by private carriage

notes.front: Where must the shipping paper be when the driver is at the vehicle’s controls?
notes.back: Within reach while belted in, and either readily visible to someone entering the cab or in the driver’s door holder.
notes.explanation: Both conditions apply together: within reach, and either visible or in the door holder.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 177 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 177.817(e)(2)(i), PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: (i) When the driver is at the vehicle’s controls, the shipping paper shall be: (A) Within his immediate reach while he is restrained by the lap belt; and (B) either readily visible to a person entering the driver’s compartment or in a holder which is mounted to the inside of the door on the driver’s side of the vehicle.

notes.front: Where must the shipping paper be when the driver is not at the vehicle’s controls?
notes.back: In the holder on the inside of the driver’s door, or on the driver’s seat.
notes.explanation: These are the only two places § 177.817(e) allows while the driver is away from the controls.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 177 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 177.817(e)(2)(ii), PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: (ii) When the driver is not at the vehicle’s controls, the shipping paper shall be: (A) In a holder which is mounted to the inside of the door on the driver’s side of the vehicle; or (B) on the driver’s seat in the vehicle.

notes.front: A driver carries the hazmat shipping paper among other papers. How must it be made to stand out?
notes.back: By tabbing it distinctively, or by having it appear first.
notes.explanation: Section 177.817(e) requires the paper to be readily available to, and recognisable by, authorities after an accident or at an inspection.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 177 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 177.817(e)(1), PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: readily available to, and recognizable by, authorities in the event of accident or inspection. Specifically, the driver and the carrier shall: (1) Clearly distinguish the shipping paper, if it is carried with other shipping papers or other papers of any kind, by either distinctively tabbing it or by having it appear first; and

notes.front: A driver stops for lunch and leaves the hazmat shipping paper in a folder in the glovebox of the locked cab. Where should it be?
notes.back: D: In the holder on the driver’s door, or on the driver’s seat.
notes.choices:
A) In the sleeper berth
B) In the glovebox, since the cab is locked
C) In the driver’s pocket
D) In the holder on the driver’s door, or on the driver’s seat
notes.choicesExplained: B: The glovebox is not one of the allowed places, locked or not. C: The paper must stay in the vehicle, in the door holder or on the seat. A: The sleeper berth is not an allowed place.
notes.explanation: With the driver away from the controls, § 177.817(e)(2)(ii) names only those two places.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 177 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 177.817(e)(2)(ii), PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: (ii) When the driver is not at the vehicle’s controls, the shipping paper shall be: (A) In a holder which is mounted to the inside of the door on the driver’s side of the vehicle; or (B) on the driver’s seat in the vehicle.

notes.front: Can a hazardous waste manifest serve as the shipping paper?
notes.back: Yes, if it contains all the information the shipping paper subpart requires.
notes.explanation: The shipping description for a hazardous waste must still be modified as § 172.101(c)(9) requires.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.205(h)–(i), PDF p. 243
notes.evidence: (h) A hazardous waste manifest required by 40 CFR part 262, containing all of the information required by this subpart, may be used as the shipping paper required by this subpart. (i) The shipping description for a hazardous waste must be modified as required by § 172.101(c)(9).
